question: packaging-retention
summary: The evidence points to a narrow, paid first step followed by a small recurring care contract, not a big custom build. Service buyers now mostly buy ringfenced, limited-scope AI work (81% paid for AI consulting in the past year; 66% bought small-scale testing help), while only about 5% of custom AI tools in one MIT study reached production, so the pilot has to be scoped to one workflow and sold with written success criteria. On the money side, agencies lose heavily to unbilled scope (57% lose $1,000-$5,000 a month; 78% rarely or only sometimes charge for out-of-scope work) and only 16% bill fully upfront, which argues for fixed-fee pilots, deposits and explicit exclusions. Retention is a process problem: 68% of 778 agencies lost clients in 2024, fewer than half have a formal anti-churn program, and longer-tenured clients correlate with structured onboarding, named ownership, agreed KPIs and regular business reviews. The main pricing constraint for this market is that small firms' median annual AI tool spend is just under $1,000, so any care fee larger than that has to be sold as labour and outcomes, not as 'AI'.

findings.finding: Client loss is normal in agency-type services and got worse in 2024, and most firms still have no formal retention system.
findings.evidence: In a survey of 778 agency leaders fielded 13 Nov-31 Dec 2024 (margin of error +/-3.4 points), 68% said they lost clients in the last year, up from 56% in 2023; 24% cited risk of client defection as a severe challenge versus 11% in 2023; the report states that 'fewer than half' have specific programmes to minimise client defection.

findings.finding: Growing revenue from existing clients is the weakest skill in these firms, which is exactly the skill a setup-plus-care model depends on.
findings.evidence: Only 7% of 778 agency leaders said their agency is extremely effective at getting existing clients to increase spending year over year; even in the best-performing 'Loyalty Builders' segment only 15% said they were very effective.

findings.finding: Retainer relationships typically last years when the firm runs a real account process, but roughly a quarter of retainer clients are gone within 12 months.
findings.evidence: Among 165 agency leaders, 42% reported average retainer tenure above two years and 30% above three years, while 5% reported under six months and 18% reported 6-12 months (about a quarter under one year); the page states its respondents were asked how long their average retainer engagement lasts, not to calculate a retention rate.

findings.finding: The retention levers that correlate with longer tenure are operational: onboarding access, named ownership, agreed KPIs and formal reviews.
findings.evidence: Promethean Research reports that agencies with formal onboarding, quarterly business reviews, dedicated account managers and agreed client KPIs retain clients longer; 62% of agency leaders said delays getting access to client systems during onboarding hurt client confidence and 60% said those delays damage the relationship if not resolved quickly; clients who arrived via referral stayed 1.9 times longer than clients won through events, networking or outbound.

findings.finding: Unbilled out-of-scope work is the norm and costs agencies four figures a month.
findings.evidence: Ignition's survey of 273 agency managers and executives found 57% lose $1,000-$5,000 per month on unbilled projects and tasks, 30% say scope creep costs more than $5,000 a month, and 78% rarely or only sometimes charge for out-of-scope work.

findings.finding: Billing in arrears is the default in agency work, and it produces predictable late payment.
findings.evidence: Only 16% of surveyed agencies require full payment upfront while 49% request partial payment in advance; 71% said at least one in four invoices is paid late; 56% said late invoices typically take two weeks to two months past the due date to collect; 84% spend at least 3-10+ hours a month chasing late payments.

findings.finding: Productised and subscription packaging is already mainstream among agencies, but almost nobody runs a single pricing model.
findings.evidence: Ignition reports 28% of agencies use hourly billing as the majority model, 28% use productised, subscription-based or tiered packages, 25% use project-based pricing and 10% use retainers. Promethean's report likewise finds 28% of agencies use a time-and-materials plus fixed-bid plus retainer mix, and only 4% or fewer rely on any single model exclusively.

findings.finding: Fixed-fee work shifts scoping risk onto the seller, which is why published guidance pairs it with tight scope definition.
findings.evidence: Promethean's pricing-method definitions state that with fixed-fee/project pricing 'the bulk of the risk of these engagements lies with the agency, as scoping inaccuracies can easily erode margins', and that the model is most appropriate when scopes are predictable and well-defined; the report puts the 2024 average agency net margin at 14% against an average of about 16% across 2015-2024.

findings.finding: Narrow positioning pays: specialists grow faster and are described as harder to replace.
findings.evidence: 84% of agencies identify as specialists (77% by service mix, 57% by industry); the report states specialists in its surveys 'consistently grow faster than generalists' and grew 43% faster than average in 2024, attributing part of this to sharper positioning and to clients sticking around longer because specialised agencies are harder to replace. Fast-growing agencies also completed 24% more projects while serving 16% fewer retainer clients than average.

findings.finding: Annual logo churn of 1-5% is the most common band for managed service providers, and most MSPs do not even measure it. Rated Medium, not High: the chapter discloses no respondent count or methodology, and MSPs are IT service providers rather than AI consultancies, so this is an analogue.
findings.evidence: ScalePad's 2026 MSP Trends Report chapter data shows 11% of MSPs lose no clients, 45% lose 1-5% a year, 27% lose 6-10%, 12% lose 11-20%, 3% lose 21%+ and 2% do not know; client churn is the top growth challenge for 26% of MSPs; only 35% track client churn as a key revenue metric; 60% have formal Customer Success programmes. Lower-churn MSPs are more likely to use structured onboarding, formal account management, monthly or quarterly QBRs and 1-2+ year client roadmaps. The page states no sample size, fieldwork dates or methodology.

findings.finding: CSAT does not reliably predict whether a small-business client stays; the buying decision sits with the owner, not ticket submitters.
findings.evidence: ScalePad reports that MSPs with best-in-class CSAT scores are more likely to report either almost no churn or higher-than-average churn, and notes CSAT is a point-in-time score from users while buying decisions are made by senior stakeholders who are not responding to automated ticket surveys.

findings.finding: Small and mid-sized businesses leave service providers mainly over price, fit and account treatment, not technology failure.
findings.evidence: JumpCloud's survey of more than 600 IT professionals at SMEs found the reasons SMEs stopped using an MSP were: became too expensive 28%, outgrown the MSP's services 26%, poor customer service or bad experience with the account/sales team 23%, MSP offered more than needed 21%, MSP no longer supported the products they wanted 18%, felt too small to be taken on 16%. 76% of SMEs rely on an MSP for at least some functions and 67% said they would increase MSP investment over the next 12 months.

findings.finding: Recurring revenue holds when the service is embedded in a control-point workflow and expands; product breadth alone does not lift gross retention.
findings.evidence: In a survey of more than 200 vertical SaaS companies (report published in 2025), median gross revenue retention was 90% for multi-product companies versus 92% for single-product companies, a 2-point gap the report reads as churn being tied to control-point stickiness rather than product breadth; median net revenue retention was 110% for multi-product versus 105% for single-product. The report's text adds that NRR for multi-product firms 'tends to exceed 100%' while many single-product firms 'hover around 100% or slightly below unless they raise prices', and that cross-selling new modules is how multi-product firms get above 100%.

findings.finding: Custom AI pilots usually die between pilot and production, and buyers say the cause is poor workflow fit rather than model quality.
findings.evidence: MIT NANDA's July 2025 report (review of 300+ public AI initiatives, 52 organisation interviews, 153 senior-leader survey responses) found that for custom or task-specific GenAI tools 60% of organisations evaluated them, 20% reached pilot and 5% reached production, i.e. 95% of organisations reported zero measurable return; top-performing mid-market firms averaged 90 days from pilot to full implementation versus nine months or more for enterprises; external partnerships saw twice the success rate of internal builds; buyers prioritised trust, understanding of their workflow, minimal disruption to current tools, clear data boundaries and the ability to improve over time.

findings.finding: Small businesses are deploying AI but spend very little on AI tools directly, which caps what a pure 'AI' fee can be.
findings.evidence: SBE Council's Small Business Technology Use Survey 2025 (532 owners of firms with 2-99 employees, fielded 12-19 March 2025, credibility interval +/-4.3 points) found 58% of small businesses are actively deploying AI tools, the median annual spend on AI is just under $1,000, 96% of those who deployed will continue investing, and 70% plan to increase spend.

findings.finding: Demand exists for small, ringfenced AI engagements rather than large transformations.
findings.evidence: Source Global Research reports 81% of clients say they have paid for consulting support on AI in the past 12 months and 99% expect to use AI advisors in the next 12 months; 66% have used small-scale support to test the potential of the technology, 54% bought a limited-scope project addressing a specific problem and 71% worked with consultants on a large project with a well-defined goal; informal, unpaid discussions were a relatively small slice.

findings.finding: A published example of the pilot-to-care ladder: fixed 10-day pilot, 50% upfront, pilot fee credited to rollout, then monthly care with a three-month minimum.
findings.evidence: Skcript's public pricing page lists a US price of USD 7,500 for a fixed 10-day AI pilot, check-ups from USD 4,000, and a 4-6 week rollout priced after the pilot; 50% is due upfront on check-ups and pilots (rollouts billed in stages); the check-up fee counts toward a pilot and the pilot fee toward the rollout if the client starts within 30 days; ongoing care is monthly with a three-month minimum, optional and unpriced; the page argues 'open-ended discovery phases are where budgets disappear'.

resources.name: NJSBDC counselling and training (New Jersey Small Business Development Center)
resources.what_it_offers: One-on-one consulting, training programmes and workshops for New Jersey small businesses via 100+ staff and consultants and seven regional centers hosted at public colleges and universities; the state office sits at the Rutgers Business School in Newark. All clients must complete an eRFC (electronic Request for Counseling) form before receiving any consulting services.
resources.cost: NJSBDC states: 'Nearly all of our services are provided at no cost through funding from federal, state, and local grants'
resources.how_to_use_it: Start by filing the eRFC request-for-counseling form, then ask for a virtual appointment with the regional center covering Middlesex County; bring the draft price card, a care-fee cost-to-serve model and a 12-month cash-flow plan to the session.

resources.name: NJSBDC at Rutgers University-New Brunswick (the center serving Middlesex County)
resources.what_it_offers: The regional center page says it 'offers training and counseling to small business owners and entrepreneurs' and that, because the Middlesex office is currently not offering in-person appointments, 'business counseling and training services remain fully operational and available virtually'. Contact published as (609) 789-8364 / rutgersnb@njsbdc.com, Monday-Friday 8:30 AM-4:30 PM.
resources.cost: Not stated on this page (the no-cost statement is published on the NJSBDC about page)
resources.how_to_use_it: This is the center to route a Middlesex County request to; use its Consulting Request Form link, expect remote-only delivery, and book within the published Monday-Friday 8:30-4:30 window, which matters for a founder with a day job.

resources.name: SCORE business mentoring (via SBA resource partners)
resources.what_it_offers: Volunteer mentors giving area-specific advice at no cost via email, telephone and video, plus training, webinars, on-demand courses and an online resource library.
resources.how_to_use_it: Use a mentor with professional-services or B2B sales background as a monthly sounding board on proposal wording and pricing conversations, and to review a standard pilot agreement before it goes to a law firm buyer.

resources.name: Agency Core 2025 Research Report (executive summary PDF)
resources.what_it_offers: Free, ungated survey of 778 small and mid-sized agency leaders on client loss, retention programmes, upsell effectiveness, pricing pressure and AI; includes segment benchmarks and a link to an interactive data dashboard.
resources.cost: Free (the report states 'No gates. No gimmicks. Just the data agency leaders need, completely free')
resources.how_to_use_it: Pull the client-loss and upsell-effectiveness figures as the baseline this consultancy must beat; use the 'Loyalty Builders' behaviours as a checklist for the care-fee scope.

resources.name: Promethean Research 2025 Digital Agency Industry Report
resources.what_it_offers: 55-page free PDF on agency pricing models, hourly rates, margins, recurring-revenue mix, specialisation and service trends, compiled from surveys conducted 2015-2025 with 1,062 agency respondents plus interviews and public data; reuse is permitted with attribution.
resources.how_to_use_it: Use the pricing-method definitions and the fixed-fee risk note to write the pilot's scope and exclusions, and the specialist-vs-generalist margins to justify staying vertical (law firms, home services) rather than selling generic AI.

resources.name: ScalePad 2026 MSP Trends Report - Customer Success + Services chapter
resources.what_it_offers: Free online chapter with client-churn distribution, CSAT limitations, the churn-reduction checklist, QBR cadence data and Customer Success programme adoption among MSPs; the page does not publish its sample size or methodology.
resources.cost: Free to read on the web
resources.how_to_use_it: Copy the churn-reduction checklist into the monthly care-fee scope (outcome reporting, published SLAs, monthly QBRs, client health tracking) and use the 1-5% annual churn band as a loose operating target, remembering it describes IT MSPs rather than AI consultancies.

resources.name: MIT NANDA 'The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025'
resources.what_it_offers: Free 26-page report on why AI pilots stall, the pilot-to-production funnel, what buyers evaluate, and why external partners outperform internal builds.
resources.how_to_use_it: Design every pilot around the buyer criteria listed in the report (workflow fit, minimal disruption, data boundaries, measurable improvement) and quote the 90-day pilot-to-implementation timeline when proposing the rollout step.

resources.name: SBE Council Small Business Technology Use Survey 2025 (release + PDF)
resources.what_it_offers: National survey of 532 small-business owners (2-99 employees) on AI deployment, AI spend, use cases, savings and reinvestment.
resources.how_to_use_it: Use the median AI spend (just under $1,000 a year) and the top use cases (content, email automation, customer support) to position the offer as replacing admin labour rather than adding another software subscription.

resources.name: Skcript public AI consulting pricing page
resources.what_it_offers: A competitor-style published price ladder: fixed 10-day pilot, check-up, 4-6 week rollout and optional monthly care, with payment terms and what is excluded.
resources.how_to_use_it: Use as a structural template (fixed price, 50% upfront, fee credited to rollout within 30 days, monthly care with a minimum term) rather than as evidence of market rates; it is one vendor's undated marketing page.

resources.name: Ignition 2025 Agency Pricing & Cash Flow Report (press release summary)
resources.what_it_offers: Free summary of a 273-respondent survey covering scope creep losses, late payments, upfront billing practice and pricing-model adoption.
resources.cost: Free press release (the full report sits behind a download page)
resources.how_to_use_it: Use it to justify contract terms internally: deposit at signing, auto-charge on the care fee, and a change-order clause for anything outside the pilot's named workflow.

recommendations_for_us: Inference: make the paid pilot the product, priced as a fixed fee for one named workflow with a written success test, following the published Skcript ladder ($7,500 for a 10-day US pilot, 50% upfront, fee credited to rollout within 30 days) and Source Global's finding that 66% of clients buy small-scale testing help. Rationale: only 5% of custom AI tools reach production (MIT NANDA), so an open-ended 'AI project' is likely to stall and take the relationship with it.

Inference: set the pilot fee from our own judgement rather than claiming a market rate, because no published benchmark for small-firm AI pilot fees was found; the only public anchor is one vendor's ladder (Skcript: check-ups from USD 4,000, 10-day pilot USD 7,500), so start nearer the check-up end and keep the care fee as a separate, smaller line (our working assumption: a few hundred to roughly $1,500 a month) rather than bundling everything into one large monthly number. Rationale: median small-business AI tool spend is just under $1,000 a year (SBE Council), so a care fee above that has to be carried by a labour-replacement and outcome story; treat both figures as hypotheses to test on the first three buyers.

Inference: charge a set-up fee and take a deposit at signing, with automatic monthly billing, instead of invoicing in arrears. Rationale: only 16% of agencies require full upfront payment and 71% say at least one in four invoices is paid late (Ignition); a one-person side business cannot absorb that cash-flow drag.

Inference: productise the delivery but write the exclusions into the pilot agreement: named workflow, included revisions, integration limits, client responsibilities, response times, and a change-order rule for anything else. Rationale: 78% of agencies rarely or only sometimes bill out-of-scope work and 30% lose more than $5,000 a month to it (Ignition), and fixed-fee work puts scoping risk on the seller (Promethean).

Inference: build the retention routine before the first client lands - onboarding access checklist, named owner (the founder), KPI baseline agreed in writing, monthly 30-minute business review, quarterly outcome report. Rationale: 62% of agency leaders say onboarding access delays hurt client confidence and firms with formal onboarding, QBRs, named account managers and agreed KPIs retain longer (Promethean); lower-churn MSPs run the same motions (ScalePad, Medium-strength analogue evidence).

Inference: sell outcome reporting tied to money or hours saved, not CSAT or 'the agent answered 400 calls'. Rationale: CSAT does not reliably predict churn and buying decisions sit with owners who are not filling in ticket surveys (ScalePad); SMEs leave providers mainly over price, fit and account treatment (JumpCloud).

Inference: stay in two or three verticals (start with law firms and home-services contractors) and reuse the same workflow templates. Rationale: 84% of agencies identify as specialists, specialists grew 43% faster than average in 2024 and are described as harder to replace (Promethean), which is the cheapest form of retention available to a solo firm.

Inference: use a three-month minimum on the care fee and a 30-day window to convert the pilot to rollout. Rationale: the published Skcript offer uses both; MIT NANDA's best mid-market performers went from pilot to full implementation in about 90 days, so a short conversion window matches how successful buyers behave. Treat this as a hypothesis to test on the first three clients, not a proven rule.

Inference: measure logo churn and gross revenue retention from client one, and aim initially to keep annual logo churn inside the 1-5% band that 45% of MSPs report. Rationale: only 35% of MSPs track churn as a key revenue metric (ScalePad) and 68% of agencies lost clients in 2024 (Agency Core); a solo founder who does not measure it will not see the pattern until revenue is gone.

pitfalls.pitfall: Selling an unbounded or 'unlimited' package: without named deliverables and revision limits, the work expands until the fee is below cost, and almost nobody bills the overage.
Running a free or open-ended 'pilot' with no success criteria: custom AI pilots overwhelmingly fail to reach production, and unpaid informal advice is only a small slice of what clients actually buy.

Competing on price to win small firms: 'too expensive' is the top reason SMEs drop a provider (28%), and 21% leave because the provider offered more than they needed, so a discount buys a mismatched client rather than a loyal one.

Treating a high satisfaction score as proof the account is safe: best-in-class CSAT MSPs are as likely to have above-average churn as near-zero churn, because the owner, not the ticket submitter, decides.
Assuming retainers are the only path to growth: fast-growing agencies served 16% fewer retainer clients and completed 24% more project work than average, so a rigid all-retainer model can cap growth.
Pricing fixed-fee work from an optimistic scope: fixed-fee pricing places scoping risk on the seller and scoping errors erode margin directly, against a 2024 average net margin of 14%.
Not tracking churn or expansion: only 35% of MSPs track churn as a key revenue metric and only 7% of agency leaders say they are extremely effective at growing existing-client revenue.

caveats: The strongest samples here are marketing/creative agencies (Agency Core 778, Ignition 273, Promethean 1,062 across surveys) and IT managed service providers (ScalePad, JumpCloud). None is a sample of AI implementation consultancies, so the churn and pricing patterns are analogues, not direct benchmarks.
Promethean's recurring-revenue and tenure sections draw on 165 agency leaders, and the report itself notes its sample skews toward larger agencies than the market as a whole.
ScalePad's chapter page publishes percentages but no respondent count, fieldwork dates or methodology, so its figures are rated Medium and read as directional.

Source Global's respondents are buyers of consulting services, typically larger organisations than the 5-200 staff firms this consultancy targets; its 81%/66% figures should be read as directional for SMB demand.

SBE Council's median AI spend is spend on AI tools, not on AI services or consultants, so it constrains the 'another subscription' frame rather than proving what a firm will pay for implementation work.
MIT NANDA's funnel figures come from 300+ public initiatives, 52 interviews and 153 survey responses and its authors describe the numbers as directionally accurate rather than official reporting.
Skcript's price page is undated vendor marketing with no stated methodology; it is used only as an example of a published structure, not as evidence of market-clearing prices.

No public benchmark was found for AI pilot conversion rates or monthly care fees at 5-200 staff firms; the care-fee and pilot-fee numbers in the recommendations are the consultant's own planning assumptions, not observed market rates.
data_gaps: No reliable public benchmark for what small firms (5-200 staff) pay for an AI implementation pilot or a monthly AI care fee; the only published numbers found come from a single undated vendor pricing page.
No public survey measuring the share of paid AI pilots that convert to a recurring contract; Source Global and MIT measure different things (AI consulting spend prevalence and pilot-to-production).
The Agency Management Institute's 2025 Agency Core PDF returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch; the 68% client-loss figure was verified instead in the Agency Core executive summary PDF.
The SBE Council PDF link returned an older 2023 checkup survey when fetched, so the 2025 figures were taken from the Council's 8 April 2025 release page instead of the PDF.
SCORE's own site returned HTTP 403; its no-cost mentoring description is taken from the SBA resource-partner page.
ScalePad's chapter page gave no respondent count, so the MSP churn figures cannot be weighted against the agency samples.
No data found on month-to-month versus 12-month contract terms for micro consultancies, so the recommended three-month minimum is untested for this segment.

No first-hand founder account with audited revenue and churn numbers for a productised AI services firm was found; Designjoy-type accounts are design services and mostly report MRR snapshots without churn.
